chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
title: Hawkins's reeds and the development of his sound
summary: Hawk used hard reeds, number three and a half or four; Dance feels his sound grew stronger over the years.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Well, now, apart from mouthpieces, Hawk sort of changed his reeds, didn't he? Didn't he -- didn't he sort of go in for much harder music?

Yes, he did, because being (unintelligible), Hawk, what you using? He said, using number three and a half or four. That's stiff. I used to use the three. But then the mouthpiece was open. You had to use a (unintelligible) soft reed. But he had that volume, and he used them three, three and a half. I'd use three, and I -- that was big enough. And Pres, he used to use -- we all practically used practically the same, but Hawk used the biggest (unintelligible) reeds.
But if you listen to the (unintelligible) -- now, of course, you have to make allowances too for recording --
-- change, but nevertheless those -- I mean when you'd really got it together, from the first you've got it together, slap tongue --

-- and he can flow on that instrument, well, that sound in the early days was a softer thing, rather more like Chu's, I would say. And then it seemed as the years go by, he's really getting stronger all the time, well, you know, until the end, --
Got sick, yeah. He was sick.

Well, I always think too that his lungs were hard. I don't think he -- I know some nights, you know, he -- after he played about an hour, he seemed to be able to take deeper breaths and everything. Seemed as though he couldn't expand his lungs, you know, at first. You know, lungs harden as you get older.
